title: Import tariff on domestic firm investment

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
The appropriate identification strategy for this scenario is the Difference-in-Differences (DID) method. The DID approach compares the change in outcomes over time between a treatment group (domestic steel producers) and a control group (non-metals manufacturers). The key assumption for this method is the parallel trends assumption, which posits that in the absence of treatment, the average change in the outcome variable for both the treatment and control groups would have been the same.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load necessary libraries
library(dplyr)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# Read in the CSV file
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s06_data.csv")

# Run the Difference-in-Differences regression
did_model <- lm(y ~ treated * post + treated + post, data = data)

# Output the results
summary(did_model)

# Extract the coefficient of interest (treat_x_post)
did_coefficient <- coef(did_model)["treated:post"]
cat("DID Coefficient (effect of tariff on treated group):", did_coefficient, "\n")

# Robustness check: Use robust standard errors
robust_se <- coeftest(did_model, vcov = vcovHC(did_model, type = "HC1"))
cat("Robust standard error for DID Coefficient:", robust_se["treated:post", "Std. Error"], "\n")

# Plot the coefficients and confidence intervals for visual inspection
library(ggplot2)

coef_df <- as.data.frame(robust_se)
coef_df$terms <- rownames(coef_df)
coef_df <- coef_df %>% filter(terms %in% c("(Intercept)", "treated", "post", "treated:post"))

ggplot(coef_df, aes(x = terms, y = Estimate)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Estimate - 1.96 * `Std. Error`, ymax = Estimate + 1.96 * `Std. Error`), 
                width = 0.2) +
  labs(x = "Term", y = "Coefficient Estimate", 
       title = "DID Regression Coefficients with Robust Errors") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 3. Expected Findings
We expect the DID coefficient for `treat_x_post` to be positive, indicating an increase in capital investment at U.S. domestic steel producers after the imposition of the tariff compared to non-metals manufacturers. The magnitude of this coefficient will depend on the extent to which the tariff effectively incentivizes increased investment within the steel industry, but we anticipate a modest positive effect due to increased domestic demand anticipated from the tariff.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID — treated=protected sector firms, control=unaffected manufacturers
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Tariff-protected firms increase capex relative to non-protected peers
_ground_truth.main_effect: 22% higher investment in treated firms post-tariff
